lesson.title: Finding the argument

steps.headline: An argument is a claim with reasons offered for it.

lead.text: The claim you are asked to accept is the conclusion. The claims offered as reasons for it are the premises.
Indicator words help: “since”, “because” and “after all” introduce a premise, while “so” and “thus” signal a conclusion.
Position does not decide it. A conclusion can come first, last or in the middle.
Standard form lists each premise on its own line, then the conclusion. That lets you judge the support before you argue about whether the premises are true.
A single clause can carry more than one claim, joined by “and”.

reveal.text: You just separated the reasons from the claim they back. Writing each premise on its own line, then the conclusion, is standard form.

model.passage: Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.

premises.text: Every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year.

conclusion.text: The bridge must be inspected this year.

model.passage: The vote is not valid, for the quorum is twelve members and only nine attended.

premises.text: The quorum for a valid vote is twelve members.
Only nine members attended the vote.

steps.headline: Find the argument in: “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet. After all, the roof still leaks and new paint would be spoiled.”

workedSteps.text: Ask what the passage wants you to believe. That is the conclusion: we should not repaint yet.
“After all” announces that reasons follow. List them: the roof still leaks, and new paint would be spoiled.

workedSteps.math: P1: The roof still leaks. P2: New paint would be spoiled. C: We shouldn't repaint the hall yet.

steps.headline: Find the conclusion in the council's passage about the playing field.

workedSteps.text: Look for the word that announces reasons: “after all”.
Ask which sentence the others are there to support.
The two reasons after “after all” become P1 and P2.

model.passage: The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.

premises.text: The playing field is the only open space in the ward.
Selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's planning policy.

conclusion.text: The council should not sell the playing field.

model.passage: You will be late to the meeting: the 8:10 has been cancelled, and the next train arrives after it starts.

premises.text: The next train arrives after the meeting starts.

conclusion.text: You will be late for the meeting.

lead.text: Speakers often skip a premise they think is obvious. To find it, ask what else must be true for the stated reason to support the conclusion.

reveal.text: That missing premise is the bridge. An argument with one left unstated is an enthymeme, from a term in Aristotle's Rhetoric. Supplying it can expose a weak spot: many solicitors qualified after a degree in another subject.

model.passage: Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree.

premises.text: Every solicitor has a law degree.

model.passage: The kettle is switched on at the wall, yet the water is cold after five minutes. So the kettle is broken.

premises.text: If the kettle is switched on at the wall and works, it heats the water.
The kettle is switched on at the wall.
The water is cold after five minutes.

lead.text: Long arguments often chain. A claim drawn on the way and then used as a premise for the next step is an intermediate conclusion.
Mapping the chain shows where an objection would bite.

model.passage: Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.

premises.text: A full, sealed glass bottle of water will crack in the freezer.

model.passage: Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.

premises.text: Every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year.

conclusion.text: The bridge must be inspected this year.

lesson.orientation: Separate premises from conclusion, write an argument in standard form and supply a missing premise.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Maya says: “We should eat early. The film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away.”

intro.promise: By the end you'll pick out the premises and conclusion in a passage, set them out in standard form and spot a premise left unsaid.
intro.whyItMatters: Every disagreement you meet is easier to settle once you can see exactly what is being claimed and why.

recap.keyIdea: An argument is a conclusion backed by premises. Find the conclusion, then list the reasons offered for it, including any left unsaid.

blocks.text: You counted the reasons in a bridge inspection passage, found a conclusion that came before its reasons, and supplied the bridge in Mira's argument.

recap.nextHook: Once an argument is laid out, you can ask whether its premises would guarantee its conclusion.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Since the bridge was built before 1950, and every bridge built before 1950 must be inspected this year, the bridge must be inspected this year.' How many premises does this argument state?
hints: Find the claim the passage wants you to accept; that is the conclusion.
'Since' introduces the reasons. List each separate claim it introduces.
Count the claims offered as reasons, leaving out the conclusion.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the bridge's date of construction, and the rule that bridges of that age must be inspected this year. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Two premises support one conclusion. The “since” clause holds both reasons, and the final clause is the claim.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion. Count only the claims offered as reasons for it.
Look at the “and” in the “since” clause. It joins two separate claims, each offered as a reason.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the conclusion of: 'The council should not sell the playing field. After all, it is the only open space in the ward, and selling a ward's only open space breaks the council's own planning policy.'?
hints: Ask which sentence the others are offered to support.

acceptedIdeas: The council should not sell the playing field
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'After all' introduces the reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

choices.label: The council should not sell the playing field
The field is the only open space in the ward
Selling a ward's only open space breaks planning policy

questions.onCorrect: “After all” announces reasons, so the opening sentence is the claim they support.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are reasons offered for the claim, not the claim itself. Ask which sentence the others support.

questions.prompt: What is the traditional name for an argument that leaves one of its premises unstated?
hints: The term comes from Greek and is used of everyday arguments that skip an obvious step.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An enthymeme: an argument with a suppressed premise, such as 'Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree'.

questions.onCorrect: An enthymeme is an argument with a suppressed premise, such as Mira's.

misconceptions.feedback: A syllogism has both premises stated. The name you want is for an argument that leaves one out.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Water expands when it freezes, so a full, sealed glass bottle left in the freezer will crack; and a cracked bottle leaks, so the freezer will need cleaning.' How many conclusions, intermediate and final, does it draw?
hints: A conclusion can be used again as a premise for a later step.
Count every claim that follows a 'so'.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two. The bottle will crack (concluded from expansion), and the freezer will need cleaning (concluded from the crack and the leak).

questions.onCorrect: Two conclusions: the bottle will crack, and the freezer will need cleaning. The first becomes a premise for the second.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the last claim. The earlier “so” also draws a conclusion.
Check what follows each “so”. The water expanding is a reason, not something concluded.

questions.prompt: Read: 'Because all reptiles are cold-blooded and every snake is a reptile, and because cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun, snakes bask in the morning sun.' How many premises does it state?
hints: Find the conclusion first; it comes at the end.
Each 'because' clause can contain more than one claim joined by 'and'.
Count the separate claims offered as reasons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three premises: reptiles are cold-blooded; snakes are reptiles; cold-blooded animals bask in the morning sun. The final clause is the conclusion.

questions.onCorrect: Three premises. A single “because” clause can hold two claims, and the final clause is the conclusion.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the conclusion at the end. Count only the claims offered as reasons.
A “because” clause with “and” holds two claims, and there is a second “because” after it. Count every reason.

questions.prompt: In 'We should cancel the picnic, since the forecast says thunderstorms', which single word signals the premise?
hints: Look for the word that could be replaced by 'because'.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 'Since' introduces the reason, the forecast; the conclusion is that we should cancel.

questions.onCorrect: “Since” introduces the reason, the forecast. The conclusion is what the reason supports.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are parts of the claims. Look for the small word that points at the reason.

questions.prompt: How many separate reasons does Maya give for eating early?
hints: Which sentence is the thing she wants us to do?
The rest of what she says is there to back it up. List those claims one at a time.
Count the claims offered as support, leaving out the one they back.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two: the film starts at seven, and the restaurant is a half-hour walk away. “We should eat early” is what they support.

questions.onCorrect: Two reasons back one claim. Seeing which is which is the first move in judging any argument.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the claim Maya wants us to accept. It is what the reasons support, not one of them.
The second sentence joins two claims with “and”. Each is a separate reason.

questions.prompt: In “The shop must be shut, because the lights are off”, which part is the conclusion?
hints: Ask which claim the other part is there to support.
questions.onCorrect: The shop's being shut is the claim. The lights being off is offered as the reason for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The lights are the reason offered. A conclusion is the claim that a reason supports.
“Because” is an indicator word. It points at a reason; it is not a claim at all.

questions.prompt: Why is the sentence “We shouldn't repaint the hall yet” the conclusion?
hints: What do the other sentences do for it?

acceptedIdeas: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.

choices.label: The other sentences are offered as reasons for it.
It comes first in the passage.

questions.onCorrect: A conclusion is picked out by what the other claims do for it, not by where it sits.

misconceptions.feedback: Conclusions can come last, as in “since …” passages. Position never settles it; what the other claims do for it does.
Length has nothing to do with it. Look at what the other claims are for.

questions.prompt: Which unstated premise makes “Mira is a solicitor, so she has a law degree” work as an argument?
hints: The missing premise must link being a solicitor to having a law degree.

acceptedIdeas: Every solicitor has a law degree.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every solicitor has a law degree.

choices.label: Every solicitor has a law degree.

questions.onCorrect: That premise bridges the gap between the reason and the conclusion. Without it the step is a leap.

misconceptions.feedback: That may be true, but it does not connect being a solicitor with having a degree.
That runs the wrong way. It starts from law graduates, but Mira is introduced as a solicitor.
